title: Meeting Rooms II
description: Find the minimum number of rooms needed to host all overlapping meetings, using a min-heap of end times.

blocks.text: Given an array of meeting time intervals, each [start, end], return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that no two overlapping meetings share the same room.

blocks.caption: A min-heap of end times tracks which rooms are currently occupied, reused whenever a room frees up in time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","intervals[][] (each [start, end], can overlap)"],["Output","The minimum number of rooms needed to host all meetings without overlap conflicts"]]}

blocks.text: The number of rooms needed at any moment equals the number of meetings currently in progress. Processing meetings in START order and tracking room availability via their END times (a min-heap of end times, or equivalently a sorted event sweep) is the classic technique for "how many things overlap at once."

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This is the same overlap-counting idea as the sweep-line technique used for interval problems generally: track a running count as intervals start and stop, and the answer is the maximum count reached at any point.

Picture meetings arriving in order of their start time. For each new meeting, check if any currently-occupied room has already finished (its end time is at or before the new meeting's start time). If so, reuse that room. Otherwise, a brand new room must be opened. The total rooms ever open simultaneously is the answer.

blocks.caption: A room is reused if it frees up in time; otherwise a new room opens.

items: Maintain a min-heap of end times, representing currently occupied rooms.
For each meeting, if the earliest-ending room (heap top) has already finished, reuse it (pop it); then push the new meeting's end time. The final heap size is the rooms needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Meeting","Heap top before","Room reused?","Heap after"],"rows":[["[0,30]","empty","no (new room)","[30]"],["[5,10]","30 (30 > 5, still busy)","no (new room)","[10, 30]"],["[15,20]","10 (10 <= 15, free)","yes, reuse (pop 10)","[20, 30]"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The final heap has size 2, matching the expected output. Meetings [0,30] and [15,20] both need active rooms simultaneously at time 15-20, requiring 2 rooms at that peak.

An event-sweep approach marks every start as +1 room needed and every end as -1, sorts all these events by time, and tracks the running total, with the answer being the maximum value reached. This is correct and conceptually simple.

The min-heap approach achieves the same result by directly simulating room assignment: process meetings in start order, and reuse the earliest-finishing room whenever possible rather than tracking a separate running counter, which some find a more intuitive direct simulation of the real-world room-booking process.
Create a +1 event at every start time and a -1 event at every end time, sort all events by time, and track the running sum, recording its maximum.

codes.python:
def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    if not intervals:
        return 0

    events = []
    for start, end in intervals:
        events.append((start, 1))
        events.append((end, -1))
    events.sort()

    rooms = 0
    max_rooms = 0
    for time, delta in events:
        rooms += delta
        max_rooms = max(max_rooms, rooms)

    return max_rooms


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(min_meeting_rooms([[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]))
    print(min_meeting_rooms([[7, 10], [2, 4]]))

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This is already an efficient O(n log n) solution; the heap-based version below is an alternative that more directly models room assignment, useful if the actual room bookings (not just the count) need tracking.

Sort meetings by start time. Maintain a min-heap of currently-occupied rooms' end times. For each meeting, if the room with the earliest end time has already finished (its end <= the new start), reuse that room (pop it from the heap); then push the new meeting's end time onto the heap. The heap's final size is the number of rooms needed.

items: Sort meetings by start time, O(n log n).
For each meeting, check and possibly pop the heap's earliest-finishing room, O(log n).
Push the current meeting's end time, O(log n).

items: "Minimum resources to cover all overlapping intervals" is answered by tracking the peak simultaneous overlap, either via an event sweep or a min-heap of end times.
A min-heap of end times directly models "reuse the earliest-available resource," a natural simulation for scheduling problems.
Both approaches share the same O(n log n) complexity; choose based on whether the actual resource assignments (not just the count) are needed.

blocks.text: Meeting Rooms II is solved by sorting meetings by start time and maintaining a min-heap of currently-occupied rooms' end times, reusing the earliest-finishing room whenever it has already ended by the time a new meeting starts. The heap's final size gives the minimum number of rooms needed, in O(n log n) time.
